This is Horst Schulze. 

The man behind the Ritz Carlton and Capella. 

He'd spent 18 years building one of the most respected luxury hotel brands in the world, and his theory was simple:

 "the room doesn't matter as much as the person standing in it"

 So he gave every employee, from housekeeping to senior management, the authority to solve guest problems without asking permission first.

The Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company, L.L.C. became what it became partly because of that.

Then he walked away to prove the philosophy could work at a different scale.

Capella Hotels and Resorts is what came next. Smaller. 

No race for market share. No giant portfolio. Around a dozen properties, each built around the idea that service culture, not brand size, is what makes guests come back.

Capella Bangkok ranked # 1 on The World’s 50 Best Hotels in 2024. 

Travel + Leisure Co. + Leisure named Capella the best hotel brand in the world three years running, from 2023 to 2025. 

Six properties hold Forbes Five-Star ratings in 2026.

What Horst understood, and most operators still resist, is that you can train people to follow a checklist or you can train them to care about the outcome. 

Both create consistency. Only one creates loyalty.

The investment is proportional to how seriously the company takes it — which is to say, not very.

👉 A high-ACV product that needs an enterprise, high-touch motion
 
The reason it works: ABM is channel-agnostic.
 
It's not a campaign. It's a GTM system that works backwards from a list of target accounts and decides the right move for every single one.
 
So we built our 10-step ABM engine 👇
 
Step 1: ICP model
👉 Score accounts from your CRM and TAM using Claude, then backtest the model
 
Step 2: TAM map

👉 Push it all to HubSpot or Attio and auto-assign Tier 1, 2, 3
 
Step 5: Contact sourcing
👉 Decision makers, champions and influencers, verified emails and phones via Findymail and BetterContact
 
Step 6: Signal tracking
👉 Capture 1st, 2nd and 3rd party signals via Trigify.io, RB2B and LeadMagic, route to reps in Slack

👉 Roll signals into 5 stages: Identified → Aware → Interested → Considering → Selecting

I just hit 145,000 followers… but it doesn’t mean much anymore. 

I’m March this year LinkedIn changed the algorithm massively and follower count doesn’t matter like it did. 

In the early days LinkedIn showed you what was happening withing your network of professional contacts. 

Then it gave weighting to what was happening all over LinkedIn based on the engagement - likes, shares, comments, dwell-time etc. 

The engagement algorithm didn’t really know what you were saying, it just knew that it was popular. 

What changed in March? A new semantic algorithm powered by AI understands what you’re saying and who would find it interesting. 

Imagine the difference between a dating app that shows your profile to random people and a professional matchmaker who gets to know you and makes a thoughtful introduction. 

There are many implications to this change: 

- follower count doesn’t dictate reach like it once did. A fresh new account could get 100,000 views per week if it’s great content. 
- gaming the system with engagement groups is unlikely to work going forward. 
- most people will get fewer views but a higher quality audience who are right for what you’re talking about. 
- longer posts will be more likely to be read. Shorter, pithy posts will be unlike to be amplified.

My biggest takeaways from Elena Verna (Head of Growth at Lovable):

1. In AI, you now need to find product-market fit every three months. Product-market fit used to mean: build something people want, then scale it for years. In AI, the underlying technology changes so fast—and customer expectations with it—that you’re constantly re-earning that fit. Even at $200M ARR.

2. The growth playbook has fundamentally changed for AI companies. Elena has led growth at Miro, Dropbox, and Amplitude and advised dozens more companies on growth. At Lovable, she says only 30% to 40% of what she learned in 20 years still applies.

3. At Lovable, growth is driven mostly through new features, not optimizing funnels. At the fastest-growing company in history, optimization drives about 5% of their growth. The other 95% comes from launching new features and products. Small tweaks don’t move the needle when everything is changing.

4. Ship constantly, and talk about it. Lovable’s main growth and retention strategy: ship features fast enough that customers feel the product is always alive. Engineers announce their own updates. The founder tweets progress daily. This keeps users curious—and keeps competitors scrambling.

5. Give your product away like candy. AI products are expensive to run, so most companies gate them behind paywalls. Lovable does the opposite: they fund hackathons, sponsor events, and hand out free credits. They treat this spending as marketing, not cost—and it compounds through word of mouth.

6. Influencer marketing outperforms paid ads by 10x. Lovable found that short videos showing what the product can do spread faster and convert better than traditional paid advertising. Showing beats telling.

7. “Minimum viable product” is dead. Elena describes the new minimum bar as “minimum lovable product.” If the experience doesn’t delight people, they won’t tell anyone. And word of mouth is your primary engine.

8. Community isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s a key lever for growth. Lovable’s Discord has hundreds of thousands of members helping each other. This amplifies word of mouth, drives retention, and makes customers feel like insiders. Building the product alone isn’t enough anymore—you’re building a world.

9. Hire people who create clarity from chaos. Fast-moving AI companies don’t have neat job descriptions or stable roadmaps. Elena looks for high-agency people who thrive in mess, including new graduates who are AI-native and former founders who know how to operate without instructions.

10. You can work at one of the fastest-growing companies in history and still see your kids. Elena wakes at 6 a.m. Stockholm time, protects her gym and family hours, and refuses to treat burnout as a badge of honor. Her point: if you set boundaries, the work will fill the available time—not all the time. | 207 comments on LinkedIn

In the last 3 months at Ahrefs, we analyzed over 1 billion data points across 11 studies*. Here's what we learned about AI search optimization:

1. YouTube mentions are the single strongest predictor of AI visibility (correlation: 0.737) – stronger than Domain Rating, backlinks, or any traditional SEO factor. YouTube is heavily cited in AI responses, and both Google and OpenAI train on YouTube content.

2. For a given query, AI Mode and AI Overviews reach the same conclusions 86% of the time – but cite almost entirely different sources (only 13.7% citation overlap). AI Mode responses are 4x longer and mention 3x more entities.

3. Content length has essentially zero correlation with AI citations (0.04). 53% of all AI Overview citations go to pages under 1,000 words. Writing ultra-long contentisan't necessary for AI visibility.

4. Google still sends 345x more traffic than ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity combined – but ChatGPT accounts for 80%+ of all AI-driven website traffic.

5. AI Overviews have a 70% chance of changing from one observation to the next, with content lasting an average of just 2.15 days. But semantic meaning stays remarkably consistent (0.95 cosine similarity).

6. "Best X" blog lists make up 43.8% of all page types cited in ChatGPT responses. 35% of those lists come from low-authority domains.

7. 79% of blog lists cited by ChatGPT were updated in 2025, and 76% of top-cited pages were refreshed within the last 30 days. Freshness matters more than ever.

8. When asked questions without valid answers, AI systems choose fabricated content with specific numbers almost every time. ChatGPT resisted best (84% accuracy), but Grok and Copilot were fully manipulated.

9. Domain Rating correlates weakly with AI visibility (just 0.266-0.326 across platforms). Number of site pages is even weaker at 0.194.

10. 67% of ChatGPT's top 1,000 citations are essentially off-limits to marketers – Wikipedia alone accounts for 29.7%, followed by homepages (23.8%) and educational content (at just 19.4%).

Anthropic just bought a Super Bowl ad to say they’ll never run ads.

There are four spots in the campaign. This one’s my favourite.

A guy doing pull-ups asks how to get a six-pack. Good advice at first, then it pivots into a pitch for insoles so “short kings can stand tall.”

Punchline: “Ads are coming to AI. But not to Claude.”

Three weeks ago OpenAI announced ads in ChatGPT. Anthropic’s response? Spend millions on the biggest ad slot in the world to say they’ll never do the same.

Mother absolutely nailed the creative. Too many tech brands default to bland purpose-driven nonsense, or worse: a laundry list of features.

This differentiates on something real, highlighting a product decision that actually matters to users.

But here’s what makes it really smart.

Anthropic’s argument isn’t just “ads are annoying.” It’s that AI conversations are fundamentally different to search or social. People share more with a chatbot than they ever would with Google. Ads in that context don’t just interrupt, they erode trust.

And this line from their blog stuck with me: “The most useful AI interaction might be a short one.”

That’s the opposite of every ad-funded platform ever built!

Of course, it helps that Anthropic’s revenue is enterprise-heavy while OpenAI is burning cash.

It’s easier to be principled when your business model allows it. But that doesn’t make it less smart.

“We won’t show you ads” isn’t an aspiration or a brand value. It’s a product decision with real revenue consequences. And that’s what makes it very hard to compete with. | 57 comments on LinkedIn
